body:
**Short answer:** yes, children can join some Santorini wine experiences — but definitely not all of them.

Some shared wine tours are strictly 18+. Some operators accept children only on private tours. Individual wineries may welcome families, while offering absolutely nothing designed to entertain a child.

So I would not ask only:

**“Are children allowed?”**

I would ask:

**“Will this actually be a good four or five hours for my child?”**

That is a much more useful question.

## “Children allowed” and “family-friendly” are not the same thing

This is the biggest booking trap.

A winery can welcome children and still offer an experience built entirely around adults sitting at a tasting table.

Estate Argyros, for example, explicitly welcomes children on its winery tours.

But the winery is equally clear about something else:

there is no playground and there are no children's activities.

Parents are expected to supervise their children and bring something quiet to keep them occupied.

I like that honesty.

It tells you far more than a little “family-friendly” icon on a booking page.

## Shared wine tours may be adults-only

Do not assume that because a winery admits children, every tour visiting that winery does too.

Tour operators set their own rules.

Santorini Wine Adventure currently makes the distinction very clearly.

Its small-group wine tours are for guests aged 18 and over.

Children and teenagers can join its private wine tours instead.

The company says under-18s can join those private tours free of charge.

So a family searching the same wineries may get two completely different answers depending on whether they choose shared or private.

That is why I would always check the **tour policy**, not just the winery policy.

## Private solves one problem — but not necessarily boredom

A private wine tour is the obvious solution if you genuinely want a wine-focused day with children.

You control the group.

The pace is easier to adjust.

There are no strangers waiting while somebody needs the bathroom, a snack or ten minutes outside.

Some private operators also allow families where their shared departures do not.

But private does not magically make three winery tastings interesting to an eight-year-old.

If your child is happy drawing, reading, listening to the guide and exploring vineyards with you, that may be fine.

If they are already bored after ten minutes of adults discussing Assyrtiko, paying more for privacy does not solve the underlying problem.

[Santorini First Visit Private Tour with Wine Tasting](https://www.viator.com/tours/Santorini/Santorini-4-Hours-Private-Experience/d959-69212P6?pid=P00320497&mcid=42383&medium=link&medium_version=selector "affiliate-button")

## A winery visit can work better than a full wine tour

This is the option I think families sometimes overlook.

Instead of spending four or five hours moving through three wineries, visit **one** winery properly.

Estate Argyros has a short introductory experience lasting around 45 minutes.

It includes a walk through the vineyards and production area followed by a tasting for the adults.

Children are welcome under supervision.

That is a much easier commitment than asking a child to sit through an entire half-day wine itinerary.

If your real goal is simply:

**“I want to understand Santorini wine and taste Vinsanto while I am here”**

you may not need a full tour at all.

## The Wine Museum changes the equation

Koutsogiannopoulos Wine Museum is more interesting from a child's point of view because there is actually something to explore.

The museum is built into a cave-like underground space and tells the history of winemaking on Santorini through exhibits and displays.

Its official FAQ explicitly says the museum welcomes **all ages**.

That gives the family two parallel experiences:

the adults get the wine context and tasting;

the child gets a museum rather than another tasting table.

That is a much stronger family proposition.

It does not guarantee every child will love it.

Nothing does.

But there is at least an experience designed around looking, moving and discovering.

## Sometimes the best wine tour for a family is not really a wine tour

This is where the research changed my view.

If I were travelling with a school-age child, I would seriously compare a farm-and-cooking experience before booking a classic three-winery tour.

One current Santorini experience combines:

* a traditional farm
* local food
* a hands-on cooking class
* wine tasting for the adults
* a maximum group of 12
* around four and a half hours

Children can participate when accompanied by an adult.

Recent family reviews describe the cooking and agricultural side as a major reason the day worked so well.

That makes sense.

The child is not tagging along with the adults' activity.

They have their own activity too.

## My family pick: farm, cooking and wine

### Santorini Family Farm Food & Wine Tour with Cooking Class

This is the first option I would compare for a family with a school-age child.

The current itinerary is around 4 hours 30 minutes and combines local agriculture, cooking, food and Santorini wine.

Instead of asking a child to behave through three consecutive tastings, the day keeps changing.

There is food.

There is cooking.

There is movement.

There is a farm.

And there is still wine for the adults.

The group is currently limited to 12 travellers.

One practical detail matters:

hotel pickup is offered, but the current Viator listing says it costs extra rather than being included in the base booking.

So check the transport cost before deciding that the headline price works for you.

**Viator product code: 35073P4**

\[AFFILIATE LINK — Santorini Family Farm Food & Wine Tour with Cooking Class]

## If you want Santorini sightseeing as well

### Santorini First-Time Visitors Private Tour with Wine Tasting

This is a very different product, and for some families it makes more sense.

It is private.

It currently lasts around four to five hours.

The itinerary combines Santorini sightseeing with one winery stop at Estate Argyros rather than making wine the entire day.

Current stops include places such as Oia, Kamari Beach and Profitis Ilias, plus the winery.

Children can participate when accompanied by an adult, and the listing says infant seats are available.

The itinerary can also be customised.

That combination is important.

A child gets villages, views and a beach stop.

The adults still get their Santorini wine tasting.

I would choose this over a pure wine tour if wine matters to you but is not the only reason for the day.

**Viator product code: 69212P6**

\[AFFILIATE LINK — Private Santorini Sightseeing Tour with Wine Tasting]

## What about babies and toddlers?

This needs a different decision.

For a baby or toddler, I would care much less about the winery name and much more about:

* total duration
* time in the vehicle
* infant seat availability
* whether a stroller works at the stops
* how easily you can shorten the day
* pickup point
* shade and heat
* whether you are locked into a group schedule

A private sightseeing-plus-wine format is usually easier to adapt than a shared tasting tour.

But do not assume a car seat is automatically provided.

If the listing says infant seats are available, request one explicitly and confirm it.

## Pickup in Oia can be different from “hotel pickup”

This is another detail worth checking.

Parts of Santorini — especially caldera-side accommodation and pedestrian areas — cannot be reached directly by vehicle.

Santorini Wine Adventure, for example, explains that when accommodation cannot be reached by car, guests meet the vehicle at a nearby accessible point.

That matters more with a child, stroller, bag and summer heat than it does for two adults carrying nothing.

So when a tour says **hotel pickup**, ask:

**“Will you collect us at our actual hotel, or at the nearest vehicle-accessible meeting point?”**

Those are not always the same thing.

## Ask about the child seat before paying

Do not assume that “children welcome” means the vehicle automatically carries the right seat.

Some current private Santorini tours specifically list infant seats.

Others do not.

Send the child's age before booking and ask the operator to confirm what will actually be provided.

For a small child, that question matters more than whether the tour pours ten wines or twelve.

## What does the child drink?

Another surprisingly useful question.

Wine-tour descriptions naturally focus on the adults.

They may say almost nothing about children.

If non-alcoholic drinks, juice or snacks matter, ask before booking.

Do not translate:

**“children accepted”**

into:

**“a children's alternative is included.”**

Unless the operator says so, we do not know.

## Who should choose what?

### Choose a private wine tour if…

Your child or teenager is comfortable with adult-focused activities.

Wine is genuinely one of the main reasons for your day.

You want flexibility.

You want to ask detailed questions and spend proper time at wineries.

And the operator explicitly confirms that under-18s are accepted.

### Choose one winery independently if…

You mainly want to understand Santorini wine.

Your child is young.

You do not want to commit half a day.

A 45–90 minute winery visit may give you most of what you want without testing everybody's patience.

### Choose the Wine Museum if…

Your child likes museums, underground spaces or seeing how things were made.

You want some wine history without building the entire day around tasting.

### Choose farm + cooking + wine if…

You have a school-age child who wants to **do something**.

For many families, this is the format I would look at first.

The adults still get local wine.

But wine is not the child's problem to endure.

### Choose sightseeing + one wine tasting if…

This is your first trip to Santorini.

The family wants Oia, views, villages or beaches.

The parents also want to try the wine.

This is probably the safest all-round compromise.

## What I would not book blindly

I would not book a standard three-winery shared tour simply because the booking engine allows you to add a child.

First check the operator's actual age policy.

Then ask what the child will be doing.

I would also be cautious about interpreting a private listing as automatically family-friendly.

One current private Santorini wine tour, for example, is private, stroller accessible and even lists infant seats — but its published minimum age is 18.

Private does not automatically mean children are allowed.

Read the actual rules.

## Five questions to send before booking

You can copy this:

> We are travelling with a child aged __. Can you confirm that they are allowed on this specific departure? Is a child seat or booster available if needed? What non-alcoholic drinks or food are included for them? How much of the tour is spent sitting at wine tastings? And if our accommodation cannot be reached by vehicle, where exactly would pickup be?

Those five answers tell you more than the words **family-friendly**.

## Dan's recommendation

I have not taken these particular tours myself.

I checked winery policies, current tour conditions and recent traveller feedback because travelling with children changes what “best wine tour” actually means.

If I were travelling with a school-age child, I would probably choose the farm-and-cooking experience.

Not because it has the most wine.

Because everybody gets something out of the day.

If this were my first family trip to Santorini, I would seriously consider the private sightseeing tour with one winery instead.

And if I simply wanted to taste Assyrtiko and Vinsanto without turning wine into a family project, I would visit Estate Argyros or the Wine Museum independently and keep the rest of the day free.

That is the distinction I would make:

**Do not ask whether your child is allowed to come.**

Ask whether you are booking a wine experience that happens to permit children — or a day your family might actually enjoy together.

## Find an experience that suits your family

You can also use the [Greece by Dan concierge](/concierge/) to compare food, wine and culture experiences by the things that actually matter to your trip.

Age rules and individual tour conditions can change, so confirm anything important directly with the operator before paying.
